pages.subtitle: The fisherman who met Jesus and ran to bring his brother.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Bethsaida, in Galilee

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Bringing people to Jesus, starting with his brother Peter

pages.intro: Andrew was a fisherman and the brother of Simon Peter. He was one of the very first people to follow Jesus. As soon as he met Jesus, he hurried to find his brother and said, "We have found the Messiah." Then he brought Peter to Jesus. All through the Gospels, Andrew keeps doing the same thing: bringing people to Jesus.
story_paragraphs: Andrew came from Bethsaida, a town in Galilee. He and his brother Simon were fishermen.

Before he met Jesus, Andrew was a follower of John the Baptist. One day, John saw Jesus walking by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God." Andrew and another disciple heard this, and they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and asked them, "What are you looking for?" They asked where he was staying. He said, "Come, and you will see." So they went and spent the rest of the day with him.

Andrew could not keep the news to himself. The first thing he did was find his brother Simon. He told him, "We have found the Messiah." Then he brought Simon to Jesus. Jesus gave Simon a new name, Peter.

Later, the two brothers were casting their net into the sea when Jesus called to them, "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men." They left their nets and followed him. Andrew became one of the twelve apostles.

One day, a huge crowd came to hear Jesus, about five thousand people, and they were hungry. It was Andrew who noticed a boy in the crowd. He told Jesus, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what good are these for so many?" Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and fed everyone. There were twelve baskets left over.

The Bible does not tell us what Andrew did after Jesus returned to heaven. Old tradition says he carried the Good News to lands around the Black Sea and to Greece, and that he died for his faith in the Greek city of Patras.
Because he was one of the first to follow Jesus, Christians in the East call Andrew "the First-Called."

pages.intro: James and his brother John were fishermen. When Jesus called them, they left their boat and their father and followed him. Jesus gave the two brothers a nickname: "sons of thunder." James was one of the three apostles closest to Jesus. He was also the first of the twelve apostles to die for his faith.
story_paragraphs: James was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee. His father was named Zebedee, and his brother was John.
One day, James and John were in their boat, mending their nets. Jesus walked along the shore and called them. They left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, and they followed Jesus.

Jesus chose twelve of his followers to be apostles, and James was one of them. Jesus gave James and John a special name. He called them Boanerges, which means "sons of thunder." Perhaps it was because the brothers had loud, bold hearts.
There were two apostles named James. This James is called "the Greater" so people can tell them apart.
James, his brother John, and Peter were often the three apostles nearest to Jesus at the most important moments of his life.

James had a lot to learn. He and his brother once hoped for the best places next to Jesus in his kingdom. Jesus asked them if they could share in his suffering. He taught his friends that being great means serving others.

After Jesus rose from the dead and returned to heaven, James helped lead the first Christians in Jerusalem. It was a dangerous time. The Bible tells us that King Herod began to harm members of the Church, and he had James, the brother of John, killed. This happened about the year 44. James was the first of the twelve apostles to die for Jesus.

A much later tradition, loved in the country of Spain, says that James once preached there, and that his body was carried to Spain after he died. Historians cannot be sure this is so. But for more than a thousand years, people have honored Saint James in the Spanish city of Santiago de Compostela. He is the patron saint of Spain.

pages.intro: Thomas was one of the twelve apostles. He is often called "Doubting Thomas," because he would not believe Jesus had risen until he saw him with his own eyes. But when Jesus came and stood in front of him, Thomas spoke some of the greatest words of faith in the whole Bible: "My Lord and my God!"
story_paragraphs: Thomas was one of the twelve apostles Jesus chose. The Gospel of John tells us he was also called Didymus, which means "the twin."

Thomas was brave. Once, Jesus wanted to go to a place where his enemies were waiting. The other disciples were afraid. Thomas said to them, "Let us also go to die with him." He was ready to stay with Jesus no matter what.

Thomas was also honest. At the Last Supper, Jesus told his friends that he was going to prepare a place for them. Thomas spoke up: "Master, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?" Jesus answered, "I am the way and the truth and the life."

Then came the hardest days. Jesus died on the cross. On Easter evening, the disciples were together behind locked doors. Suddenly Jesus stood among them and said, "Peace be with you." He showed them his hands and his side, and they were filled with joy.

But Thomas was not there. When the others told him, "We have seen the Lord," he could not believe it. He said, "Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands and put my finger into the nailmarks and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

A week later, the disciples were together again, and this time Thomas was with them. The doors were locked. Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you." Then he turned to Thomas. "Put your finger here and see my hands," he said. "Do not be unbelieving, but believe."
Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God!" Jesus said to him, "Have you come to believe because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed." Those words are for us.
A strong and very old tradition says that Thomas later traveled far to the east, all the way to India, to tell people about Jesus.

pages.intro: Philip and James were two of the twelve apostles. Philip was called by Jesus with two simple words, "Follow me," and he quickly brought a friend to meet Jesus too. James is sometimes called "James the Less." We know very little about him, but Jesus chose him, and he said yes. The Church honors these two apostles together on May 3.
story_paragraphs: When Jesus chose twelve men to be his apostles, Philip and James were both on the list. The Church remembers them on the same day.
Philip came from Bethsaida, the same town as the brothers Peter and Andrew. One day, Jesus found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." And Philip did.

Philip was so glad that he went straight to his friend Nathanael. He told him they had found the one the prophets had written about: Jesus, from the town of Nazareth. Nathanael was not impressed. He asked, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?" Philip did not argue. He just said, "Come and see."

Later, a huge crowd followed Jesus, and they were hungry. Jesus asked Philip, "Where can we buy enough food for them to eat?" Jesus was testing him. Philip answered that even two hundred days' pay would not buy enough. Then Jesus fed the whole crowd with five loaves and two fish.

At the Last Supper, Philip made a request. "Master, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." Jesus answered, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." When we look at Jesus, we see what God is like.

The other apostle in this pair is James, the son of Alphaeus. He is often called "James the Less," so that people will not mix him up with the other apostle James, the brother of John. The Bible lists him among the Twelve but tells us almost nothing else about him. He followed Jesus faithfully and quietly.
After Jesus returned to heaven, the apostles went out to share the Good News. Tradition says Philip preached in the land that is now Turkey.
Why are Philip and James honored together? Long ago, in the 500s, their relics were brought to the same church in Rome. Christians have celebrated them on one day ever since.

pages.intro: Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles. A very old tradition says he is the same person the Gospel of John calls Nathanael. At first, Nathanael did not think anyone important could come from the little town of Nazareth. Then he met Jesus. Jesus already knew him, and Nathanael believed. Jesus called him a man with no dishonesty in him.
story_paragraphs: The name Bartholomew appears in the Bible's lists of the twelve apostles. The name means "son of Tolmai." The lists do not tell us anything more about him.

But a very old tradition in the Church says that Bartholomew had another name: Nathanael. The Gospel of John tells a wonderful story about Nathanael, and Christians have long believed it is the story of how Bartholomew met Jesus.
Nathanael had a friend named Philip. One day, Philip came to him with exciting news. He said they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about: Jesus, from the town of Nazareth.
Nazareth was a small, ordinary town. Nathanael asked, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?" Philip answered, "Come and see."

So Nathanael went. As he walked up, Jesus said, "Here is a true Israelite. There is no duplicity in him." Duplicity means being dishonest or two-faced. Jesus was saying that Nathanael was an honest man who said what he really thought.

Nathanael was surprised. "How do you know me?" he asked. Jesus answered, "Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree." Nathanael was amazed that Jesus had seen him and known him. He said, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel."

Jesus told him this was only the beginning. "You will see greater things than this," he said. And he did. As one of the twelve apostles, Bartholomew stayed with Jesus, heard him teach, and saw him risen from the dead.

The Bible does not tell us what Bartholomew did afterward. Old traditions say he traveled far to share the Good News, and the strongest tradition says he brought the faith to the land of Armenia. The Church in Armenia honors him as one of its founders. Tradition also says he gave his life for Jesus.

pages.intro: Simon and Jude were two of the twelve apostles. The Bible tells us very little about them. Simon was called "the Zealot." Jude is also called Thaddeus. They were not famous like Peter or John, but Jesus chose them, and they stayed faithful to him. Today many people ask Saint Jude to pray for them when they are in great need.
story_paragraphs: One night, Jesus went up a mountain and prayed to God until morning. When day came, he called his disciples together and chose twelve of them. He named them apostles. Near the end of the list are two names side by side: Simon and Jude.

There were two apostles named Simon. One was Simon Peter. The other is the Simon we honor today. The Bible calls him "Simon who was called a Zealot." A zealot is a person who cares about something with all his heart. Simon cared deeply about his people and their faith.

Jude has more than one name in the Bible. He is called Thaddeus, and he is also called "Judas the son of James." He is not the same person as Judas Iscariot, the one who turned against Jesus. The Gospel of John is careful to say "Judas, not the Iscariot."

We hear Jude speak only once. At the Last Supper, Jesus was telling his friends that he would show himself to those who love him. Jude asked a question. He wanted to know why Jesus would show himself to them and not to the whole world. Jesus answered by speaking about love: whoever loves him will keep his word.
One short letter in the New Testament is called the Letter of Jude. Christians have traditionally said it came from this apostle.
That is nearly all the Bible tells us. Simon and Jude were with Jesus through his teaching, his death, and his rising. They received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost with the others.

What happened next is known only from tradition. Old stories say Simon and Jude traveled far to tell people about Jesus, that they worked together in the land of Persia, and that they died there for their faith. That is why they share one feast day.
Today, people all over the world ask Saint Jude to pray for them when a problem seems hopeless.

pages.intro: Matthias followed Jesus from the very beginning, though the Gospels never mention his name. After Jesus returned to heaven, there were only eleven apostles, because Judas was gone. The first Christians prayed and asked God to show them who should take that place. The one who was chosen was Matthias. He became the twelfth apostle.
story_paragraphs: Jesus chose twelve apostles. But one of them, Judas Iscariot, turned against Jesus and handed him over to his enemies. After that, Judas was gone, and only eleven apostles were left.
Jesus rose from the dead, and forty days later he returned to heaven. His followers stayed together in Jerusalem, praying. There were about 120 of them.

One day, Peter stood up to speak. He said that someone needed to take the empty place among the apostles. Peter explained what kind of person it should be. It had to be one of the men who had been with them the whole time, from the day John baptized Jesus until the day Jesus was taken up to heaven. That person would join the apostles in telling the world that Jesus is risen.
Two men were put forward. One was Joseph, who was called Barsabbas. The other was Matthias.

Both were good men who had followed Jesus faithfully. How could the group choose? They did not argue or vote for their favorite. They prayed. They asked the Lord, who knows every heart, to show them which one he had chosen.

Then they cast lots. Casting lots was a way of choosing in Bible times, a little like drawing a name. The Bible says, "The lot fell upon Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles." A few days later came Pentecost. The Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, and Matthias was with them.

Think about what this tells us. Matthias had been following Jesus all along, for years. He was not one of the famous ones, and nobody had written down his name. But he had been faithful the whole time, and God knew it.
The Bible does not tell us anything more about Matthias. Later traditions tell different stories about where he preached, and none of them is certain.

pages.subtitle: The "son of encouragement," who believed in people and gave them a second chance.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: The island of Cyprus

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Encouraging others and helping Saint Paul begin his work

pages.intro: Barnabas was one of the first Christians. His real name was Joseph, but the apostles gave him a new one: Barnabas, which means "son of encouragement." He lived up to it. When everyone was afraid of Saul, Barnabas stood up for him. When young Mark failed, Barnabas gave him another chance. He helped other people become who God wanted them to be.
story_paragraphs: Barnabas was born on the island of Cyprus. His name was Joseph. But the apostles gave him a new name, Barnabas, which means "son of encouragement." To encourage means to give someone courage and hope.

The first Christians in Jerusalem shared everything they had, so that no one among them was in need. Barnabas owned a piece of land. He sold it, brought the money, and gave it to the apostles to help the poor.
Then a man named Saul came to Jerusalem. Saul had once hunted down Christians. Now he said he believed in Jesus. The disciples were all afraid of him. They did not believe he had really changed.
Barnabas did. He took Saul to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord and had spoken boldly about Jesus. Because of Barnabas, Saul was welcomed. Saul would become the great Saint Paul.

Later, the Church sent Barnabas to the city of Antioch, where many new people were coming to believe. He was glad at what he saw, and he encouraged them all to stay faithful. The Bible says of him, "He was a good man, filled with the holy Spirit and faith."

There was so much to do that Barnabas went to find Saul and brought him to Antioch to help. They taught there together for a whole year. It was in Antioch that the followers of Jesus were first called Christians.
Barnabas and Paul then set out on a long journey to tell people about Jesus. A young helper named John Mark went with them, but he left and went home.

When it was time for another journey, Barnabas wanted to bring Mark again. Paul said no. They disagreed so strongly that they went separate ways. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus. Barnabas was right to give Mark another chance. Mark later became a trusted helper, and he wrote one of the four Gospels.

pages.subtitle: One of the first deacons, and the first person to give his life for Jesus.

quick_facts.label: Lived

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Jerusalem

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Serving the poor, and forgiving those who killed him

pages.intro: Stephen lived in Jerusalem in the first days of the Church. He was one of seven men chosen to make sure that poor widows had enough to eat. He also spoke boldly about Jesus. Some people grew so angry that they killed him. As he was dying, Stephen prayed for them. He was the first Christian to die for his faith.
story_paragraphs: After Jesus returned to heaven, more and more people in Jerusalem came to believe in him. The Christians shared their food and took care of one another.
But a problem came up. Some of the widows, women whose husbands had died, were being left out when food was given out each day.

The twelve apostles wanted to fix this. They also needed to keep praying and teaching. So they asked the community to choose seven good men, "filled with the Spirit and wisdom," to take charge of this work. The first one chosen was Stephen, "a man filled with faith and the holy Spirit." The apostles prayed and laid their hands on the seven. The Church remembers these men as the first deacons.

Stephen did more than serve meals. The Bible says he was "filled with grace and power," and he did great wonders among the people. He spoke about Jesus with so much wisdom that those who argued with him could not answer.
Some men became angry. They told lies about Stephen and brought him before the council of leaders. As everyone stared at him, they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

Stephen told them the long story of God's people. Then he looked up and said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." The crowd would not listen. They rushed at him, dragged him out of the city, and threw stones at him.

Stephen prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then he knelt down and cried out, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." With those words, he died. He had forgiven them, just as Jesus forgave from the cross.
A young man named Saul was standing there, watching over the coats of the men who threw the stones. One day, Saul would meet Jesus and become Saint Paul.

pages.subtitle: A young helper of Saint Paul, who learned his faith from his mother and grandmother.

quick_facts.label: Known for

pages.intro: Timothy grew up in a town called Lystra. His mother, Eunice, and his grandmother, Lois, taught him to love God. When Saint Paul came to town, he saw how good and faithful Timothy was, and he asked the young man to travel with him. Timothy became one of Paul's most trusted helpers. Two letters in the Bible are written to him.
story_paragraphs: Timothy lived in the town of Lystra, in the land that is now Turkey. His father was Greek. His mother was Jewish, and she had become a believer in Jesus.

Timothy first learned about God at home. His mother's name was Eunice, and his grandmother's name was Lois. Years later, a letter to Timothy remembers his "sincere faith that first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice."

When Saint Paul came to Lystra on one of his journeys, he met Timothy. The Christians in Lystra and in a nearby town all "spoke highly of him." Paul wanted Timothy to come along with him. So Timothy left home and set out with Paul.
They traveled from city to city. Everywhere they went, the churches grew stronger in faith, and more people came to believe.
Timothy became like a son to Paul. Paul trusted him with hard jobs. When Paul could not visit a group of new Christians himself, he sent Timothy to teach them and cheer them on.
Later, Timothy was given the care of the Christians in the great city of Ephesus. Early tradition honors him as the first bishop there.

Timothy was young for such a big job, and it seems he was sometimes shy. The Bible has two letters written to help him. One of them says, "Let no one have contempt for your youth, but set an example for those who believe, in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity." In other words: do not let anyone look down on you because you are young. Show everyone how to live by the way you speak and act.

Another letter reminds Timothy that God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love. Timothy stayed faithful for the rest of his life. He shares a feast day with another of Paul's helpers, Saint Titus, on January 26.

pages.subtitle: A trusted helper of Saint Paul who brought peace and put things in order.

pages.intro: Titus was one of Saint Paul's closest helpers. He was not Jewish, and he came to believe in Jesus through the first Christians. Paul sent Titus on some of his hardest jobs, because Titus knew how to make peace when people were upset. Later, Paul left him on the island of Crete to lead the Church there. One letter in the Bible is written to him.
story_paragraphs: Titus lived in the first century, in the time of the apostles. He was a Gentile, which means he was not Jewish. He became a Christian and a close friend and helper of Saint Paul.

A letter in the Bible begins with a warm greeting from Paul "to Titus, my true child in our common faith." Paul was not Titus's father. He meant that he loved Titus like a son, because they shared the same faith in Jesus.

In those early days, the Christians had a big question to settle. Did people who were not Jewish have to follow all the Jewish laws before they could follow Jesus? Paul brought Titus with him to Jerusalem when the leaders met to talk about it. The leaders agreed that Titus could be a Christian just as he was.
Paul trusted Titus with difficult jobs. One of the hardest was in the Greek city of Corinth. The Christians there had been quarreling, and they had hurt Paul's feelings. Paul sent Titus to help.

Paul waited and worried. He wrote that he was troubled on every side. Then Titus came back with good news. The people of Corinth were sorry, and they wanted to make things right. Paul wrote, "God, who encourages the downcast, encouraged us by the arrival of Titus." Titus was happy too. His heart went out to the people of Corinth.

Later, Paul gave Titus a new job on Crete, a large island in the sea. The Church there was just beginning. Paul wrote to him, "I left you in Crete so that you might set right what remains to be done." Titus was to choose good leaders for every town and to teach the people well.
Because of this, tradition honors Titus as the first bishop of Crete. It is said that he led the Church there until he was an old man and died in peace. He is the patron saint of Crete.

pages.subtitle: A friend of Jesus who welcomed him into her home and believed in him with all her heart.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Bethany, a village near Jerusalem

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Welcoming Jesus and serving others

pages.intro: Martha lived in the village of Bethany with her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus. Jesus was their close friend. Martha loved to welcome him and cook for him. Once she got so busy that she grew upset, and Jesus gently helped her see what matters most. Later, when her brother died, Martha showed how strong her faith in Jesus was.
story_paragraphs: Martha lived in Bethany, a village about two miles from Jerusalem. She shared a home with her sister, Mary, and her brother, Lazarus. The Bible tells us, "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus."

One day, Jesus came to their village, and Martha welcomed him into her home. She wanted everything to be just right for her guest. There was so much to do! But her sister Mary sat down at Jesus's feet and listened to him speak.
Martha grew upset. She came to Jesus and said, "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me by myself to do the serving? Tell her to help me."

Jesus answered her kindly. "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and worried about many things. There is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part." Jesus was not scolding Martha for working hard. He was reminding her that being with him comes first.
Some time later, Lazarus became very sick. The sisters sent a message to Jesus. But by the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had died and had been in the tomb for four days.

When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet him. She said, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you."

Jesus told her, "I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live." Then he asked, "Do you believe this?" Martha answered, "Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God."

Then Jesus went to the tomb. He had the stone taken away, and he called out in a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" And Lazarus came out, alive. Martha is the patron saint of cooks and of everyone who welcomes guests.
